items.excerpt: Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at Canadian military base EDMONTON, Alberta (AP) — Canada’s defense minister says that people have been killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire, while reports said that large numbers of injured people were being transported to hospitals. Fire crews scrambled late into the night Saturday as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area. It was not immediately clear how many people were killed or injured, but a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 120 miles northwest, told Canada’s national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health-care facilities around the base became “completely overwhelmed” by the number of people needing care. Vance faces tough questions on Iran war, immigration and more in CBS town hall WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Vice President JD Vance faced tough questions from voters about the Trump administration’s policies on data centers, high costs, immigration and his own rhetoric in a town hall on CBS News that aired Saturday night. The string of sharp queries, some from voters who said they had supported him and President Donald Trump, previewed the rocky path he may face trying to answer for the administration’s record if he runs for president himself. Blaze at St Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches more than 1,000 drones at Russia Ukrainian attacks have set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg. Kyiv launched over 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest aerial bombardments. The attack comes amid tensions between Ukraine and Washington, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. One person was killed and five were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot. Meanwhile, one woman died and at least two other people were injured after Russia launched two attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said. Hurricane Trudy brings heavy rain and strong winds to Mexico’s Pacific coast MIAMI (AP) — Hurricane Trudy brings heavy rain and strong winds to Mexico’s southwestern and west-central Pacific coast, according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center. A hurricane warning remains in effect from Manzanillo to Cabo Corrientes. On Sunday, Trudy is expected to bring 4-8 inches of rain, with isolated totals of around 12 inches. Authorities warn of potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Meanwhile, Typhoon Champi strengthened into a Category 4 super typhoon as it moved past Guam. U.S. President Donald Trump has approved an emergency declaration for Guam, authorizing FEMA to coordinate federal disaster relief efforts. Pope Leo tells faithful in St. Peter's Square he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV has thanked the faithful in St. Peter’s Square for their prayers after his hospitalization for lung surgery. Speaking from a window overlooking the square, he said he would gradually resume his activities with God's help. The pontiff had a malignant tumor removed last week and expressed gratitude to the medical staff at Gemelli hospital. He said the experience made him feel closer to those facing illness. The 71-year-old pope is recovering well and plans to continue his duties, including a scheduled trip to South America in November. His surgeon sees no clinical reasons to cancel the trip. ... Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools U.S. consumers are uneasy about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting prices. Digital price tags are replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like “dynamic pricing” and “surveillance pricing” are stirring up anger and anxiety on social media. Much of the concern focuses on whether customer data is getting used to give different people different prices for the same product. Walmart and McDonald's say critics misunderstand how their pricing tools work. Lawmakers and regulators are taking preemptive action to restrict when companies can use personal data in pricing. Paris police report 855 arrests after violent clashes and looting during protests PARIS (AP) — Paris police have arrested 855 people after violent clashes during a protest against rising living costs. The protest on Saturday drew about 110,000 people in the French capital. Authorities said masked groups targeted public buildings, including city halls. Around 550,000 people protested across France, with organizers claiming 800,000. One person died of a heart attack, and several officers and firefighters were injured. Looting and damage were reported in Paris. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu blamed “radical far-left groups” for the violence. Mayors of major cities have requested a meeting with the prime minister due to the damage. Japan to launch spacecraft on a mission to get samples from a Martian moon TOKYO (AP) — Japan is launching a spacecraft on a groundbreaking mission to bring back samples from Phobos, one of Mars' moons. Scientists hope the five-year mission will reveal how Phobos and its sibling moon, Deimos, formed, potentially shedding light on the origins of life in the solar system. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's launch on Tuesday comes as other nations consider sending astronauts to Mars. Samples from Phobos could provide valuable data for future manned missions. Japan is leading the international effort, with support from NASA and other space agencies. The mission aims to return to Earth in 2031. ... Hurricane warning: Miami poised for No. 1 after 5 of the top 7 teams lose in historic Top 25 day ... The college football rankings are in for a shakeup after a historic weekend for the Associated Press Top 25. Five of the top seven teams, including No. 1 Georgia and No. 2 Notre Dame, lost on the same day for the first time since the poll began in 1936. Miami, now 6-0, is set to take the top spot after a double-overtime win against Florida State. Ohio State, BYU, Mississippi, and Texas Tech are also eyeing promotions. The big question is how far Georgia, Notre Dame and Indiana will fall after their close losses.

items.title: Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day
items.excerpt: Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day # Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day Jared Blikre Sun, October 18, 2026 at 6:33 AM CDT 3 min read Inflation is reaching fewer corners of the economy. That doesn't mean life is getting cheaper. Only about 38% of the roughly 175 categories in the Consumer Price Index rose faster than a 3% annual pace over the past six months, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data. That's down from 56% in May and the fewest since spring 2025. The count borrows a test from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who laid it out at Jackson Hole in August. He counts how many categories in the Fed's preferred PCE price gauge are rising faster than 3%, a gauge of how widespread inflation is. The Fed's goal is still 2%. BLS, Yahoo Finance "Too many categories are still posting increases above 3% on both a six- and 12-month basis," Warsh said after the Fed raised rates in September. By that yardstick, September looked better than its hotter-than-expected headline. The 12-month count slipped to about 47% from 51% in August. At the 2022 peak, about 4 in 5 categories topped 3%. In the two decades before the pandemic, about 1 in 3 typically did. A narrower spread strengthens the case for waiting, and traders have leaned that way. The bond market put the odds of a hike at the Oct. 27-28 meeting at about 17% by Friday's close, according to Bloomberg data — down from roughly 33% after Wednesday's CPI report. Warsh declined to preview his next move in remarks Friday before the International Monetary Fund. Some Fed officials want more evidence before moving. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called September's inflation report discouraging but told Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger he favors waiting before acting again. "We need to get more data," he said. ## The holdout categories are the expensive ones Electricity, rent, hospital services, and car repairs have all been rising faster than 3% over the past six months, after adjusting for seasonal swings. Gasoline is up about 34% from a year ago. Together, the categories still above the line make up at least 60% of the CPI basket, which the BLS weights by how much households spend on each item. Groceries show the other side of the problem. Grocery prices rose less than 2% over the past year, yet they're still up nearly a third since December 2019. Electricity is up 43% over the same stretch. BLS, Yahoo Finance Slower inflation means prices rise more slowly. It doesn't bring them back down, and the Fed has no intention of returning to 2019 prices. Not everyone sees progress. "There is little evidence of a cooling or a broad-based disinflationary impulse," RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas wrote Wednesday, pointing to trade, energy, and AI as sources of stubborn price pressure. He expects another quarter-point hike in December. The bond market leans his way on the longer view. Traders still price in about one full quarter-point increase by the Dec. 9 meeting and nearly three by September 2027. The next test arrives Oct. 29, when September PCE inflation is released, one day after the Fed decides. Next month's CPI report follows. If the six-month count holds below 40%, the case for waiting gets stronger. A return to 50% or more — near where it sat for most of the first half of the year — would put a hike back on the table. Watch rent and electricity. Until they cool, a shrinking count won't feel like relief. *Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication.* *Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. Follow him on X at @SPYJared or email him at **jaredblikre@yahooinc.com**.*

items.title: Powered by spikes in energy prices, inflation surges to 3.7% - NKyTribune
items.excerpt: Spikes in energy prices were largely responsible: Gas is now up 34% for the year, and fuel oil, which includes diesel, is up 72% as the Iran war drags on. States including Georgia, Kentucky, Illinois, Indiana, North Carolina, Ohio and Utah have enacted gas tax relief measures recently to battle rising prices. North Carolina expects to lose more than $362 million in tax revenue for the fiscal year because of a gas tax holiday. New York state estimates fuel oil prices are up 67% from last year, with home heating oil at $6.21 a gallon as of this month. Connecticut announced plans Oct. 13 for additional state aid for home heating assistance, partly because of high prices for delivered oil. Other than energy, the largest factor was food away from home, up 3.5%. The only decreases were medical care products, down 3.3%, and used cars and trucks, up for the month but still down 1.5% for the year. So-called “core” inflation outside of volatile food and energy was a more modest 2.6%. Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org. items.excerpt: Retail price impacts from the Iran war are uneven but add up for US households before midterms NEW YORK (AP) — High fuel prices are making it more expensive to drive, fly and buy some goods more than seven months into the U.S.-Iran war. That's prolonging the strain on American households as the midterm elections approach., The chief economist at Moody’s Analytics estimates the war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, including $1,100 related to energy. Motorists and airline passengers so far have borne the clearest consequences from disrupted Middle East oil shipments. The elevated cost of making and moving goods hasn't translated into across-the-board retail price increases. Shoppers may not be spared indefinitely, though. U.S. consumers are uneasy about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting prices. Digital price tags are replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like “dynamic pricing” and “surveillance pricing” are stirring up anger and anxiety on social media. Much of the concern focuses on whether customer data is getting used to give different people different prices for the same product. Walmart and McDonald's say critics misunderstand how their pricing tools work. Lawmakers and regulators are taking preemptive action to restrict when companies can use personal data in pricing. BANGKOK (AP) — U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh says he won't prejudge what the U.S. central bank will do about interest rates at its upcoming meetings. However, he repeatedly vowed to “deliver price stability.” Warsh spoke Friday on the sidelines of a meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok. The global surge in prices is a key concern of the financial leaders meeting. Stubbornly high U.S. inflation is expected to lead the Fed to raise its key interest rate in coming months after a rate hike in September.

Paramount and Legendary’s Street Fighter is headed toward an estimated $31 million domestic opening, enough to put the video-game adaptation at the top of the weekend box office. Andrew Koji stars as Ryu opposite Noah Centineo’s Ken, with Callina Liang as Chun-Li and a deliberately outrageous supporting cast that includes Jason Momoa, Roman Reigns, Cody Rhodes, David Dastmalchian, 50 Cent and Eric André. The movie entered the weekend with roughly $4 million from Thursday previews before expanding into its full theatrical run.

items.title: Tini: FUTTURA World Tour | Miami & Miami Beach
items.excerpt: # Tini: FUTTURA World Tour ### Oct 18, 2026 ##### Doors open: 7:00 PM | Show starts: 8:00 PM Argentine pop artist Tini brings her FUTTURA World Tour to downtown Miami for the tour’s only U.S. stop. Tini: FUTTURA World Tour takes place Sunday, October 18, 2026 at Kaseya Center. The tour is described as a retrospective project spanning Tini’s different musical eras, from her early international breakthrough on Disney Channel Latin America’s Violetta to her solo career in pop, urbano, cumbia and alternative pop. The Miami concert follows the tour’s launch in Buenos Aires and brings the arena production to a U.S. audience for one night only. Born Martina Stoessel, Tini is an Argentine singer, actress and performer whose albums include Tini, Quiero Volver, Tini Tini Tini, Cupido and Un Mechón de Pelo. Her career includes chart success in Latin America and Europe, multiple major music awards and collaborations that have expanded her reach across Latin pop and global music audiences. The event is open to all ages, though ages 18 and older are recommended.
